The radar cross section of a half-wave dipole is derived assuming no losses in the scattering process.
The induced current on the dipole is assumed identical to that when the dipole is driven as a transmitting antenna.
The dipole length is approximately half the wavelength of the incident radar wave.
The current distribution on the dipole is sinusoidal with maximum at the center and zero at the ends.
The radar cross section varies as a function of observation angle relative to the dipole axis.
The derived RCS formula involves sinusoidal terms reflecting the current distribution along the dipole.
The RCS represents the effective scattering area that quantifies backscattered power.
The analysis neglects material and environmental losses.
The scattered fields are calculated using antenna radiation integrals based on the induced current.
The derived RCS agrees with known special cases such as normal incidence.
The half-wave dipole serves as a fundamental model for understanding radar scattering.
The paper provides explicit analytical expressions for RCS rather than numerical simulations.
The study aids in radar target identification and antenna design.
The assumption of lossless scattering simplifies the theoretical treatment.
No experimental measurements are reported in the paper.
The paper was published in the American Journal of Physics in 1970.
The author is David L. Mott from New Mexico State University.
The paper is frequently cited in radar and antenna theory literature.
The RCS pattern shows maxima and minima corresponding to the dipole's radiation pattern.
The study helps bridge antenna theory and radar cross section analysis.
